commentBody: Cruisy but interesting. Thanks!

Sean writes:

"Today, I learned about A FORTIORI, or [By an even stronger argument, at law]."

I learned about it on July 18, when it appeared in that day's puzzle, with largely the same clue.  

It also appeared in 2009, and three times before I started solving crosswords, but I don't remember the 2009 appearance, and there was no "Archive" to practice from in the 80s.

Some real highs and lows in this one. 

Highs: SPIROGRAPH crossed with NERF BALL

Lows: Clue for EGO:  “It’s mine! All mine.”

Completing this puzzle was not a SISYPHEAN task. In fact it was mostly downhill.  Lots of fresh entries made it fun though: e.g. PETRIDISH, ELCLASICO, SPIROGRAPH and the aforementioned SISYPHEAN.  I also liked the NN,EE, RR stack in the SW.

Not very hard, and nothing too cutesy or misdirecting (at least, nothing that fooled me for very long), but a pretty solid grid and a CLASS ACT. I liked the corner stacks, especially the lower right, and a lot was in my wheelhouse and brought back fond memories. Love Greek mythology. Thought the SIRENSONG clue was a little forced but any Odyssey reference is OK, and SISYPHEAN is another favorite myth of mine. Our friends overseas who get shortchanged with too many American sports references should be happy we get Cricket today and their kind of Football. Thank you perennial crossword fave Enya whose song ORINOCO Flow made that a quick fill-in with a few letters. Minor medical nit—there’s not really a “certain” coronary artery, there are many coronary arteries in the heart, so “like a certain type of artery” or “like a group of arteries” would have been better worded. Any one looking for dooks, no, the puzzle is not suggesting it is OK to WHIP PETS. Finally, what a call out to my childhood crossing NERFBALL with SPIROGRAPH. Is the latter still around? I still remember the one with pins and corrugated cardboard to keep the rings in place. I still remember the commercials: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=a1Uppffbfvw&ra=m Have a great weekend everyone!

That was challenging in parts but not too much so. Loved DOGOWNER, RELIEFMAP, WELLTODO, and KAISER.

"I finally found my map with earth's landforms!"

And had the same idea as Sean - Sisyphus trying and trying to complete a killer Saturday puzzle. He keeps getting “oh fiddlesticks” and decides to start all over. But he doesn’t give up! Because it’s his fun hobby!

That was fun. Good trivia, Orinoco especially,  and clues and answers you don't see every day -- mensch, el clasico, Sisyphean and a fortiori, which was new to me. The puzzle was almost devoid of boring old crosswordese except for SRO. Let's have more like this.
Too much trivia.
Enjoyable Friday that went fast. Fun clues.

I enjoyed this puzzle a lot--chewy but not grisly, demanding but not like my high school football coach (before he gave up on me completely).

There are roughly three ways my grid can look when I'm about half way in, timewise.

1) Nothing but completed blocs and blocs I haven't gotten to yet.
2) No section is really completed, but a lot is filled in and there are several answers which cross.
3) No section is complete, and there are vast areas of white space with a very few, uncrossed entries.

The first is easy, the third is where I usually gave up on weekends a year or two ago, and sometimes still can't pull it off.

The middle one was tonight.  I had a lot of places where I was unsure (SISIPHyAN instead of SISYPHEAN, SATay or SATIy instead of SATIE, ERICA vs. ERIkA).

Usually this kind of pattern means I'll have flyspecking to do, and tonight was no exception.  I took me a while to deal with the uncertainties in the previous paragraph.

I would have helped had I known SATIE, because it landed in all that mess.

I'm asking the Spanish speakers here:  I struggled with EL CLASICO vs EL CLASIkO.  I can't think of any Spanish words with a "K".  Are there any?  Is "K" used in Spanish?
Some good guesses for several unknowns got me a time 40% less than average. Not an easy puzzle, just less difficult for me for a Friday.
"Accounts for checking" was just one of several really great clues. The puzzle was a consistently pleasant workout.

Bravo. This one is really on my wavelength. Apologies for this self-absorbed comment but I'd like to raise a toast to the puzzle creator:

I was writing a blog post about the Sirens' Song right before I started the puzzle.
Prufrock is my favorite poem. Asahi Superdry is one of my favorite beers. I like relief maps and even have a relief globe. Wong Kar Wai is one of my favorite directors (though I prefer Days of Being Wild over Chungking Express). The Myth of Sisyphus is one of my favorite myths. I like noodles and martinis (dry though). The only sport I like to watch is international soccer. I like Dali, LOTR, and I have a dog. Look forward to your next puzzle!
Had SPITBALL my first go round, confidentially I might add!
incredible puzzle thanks Nam - this is a true words with meaning puzzle with popular references that have deeper meaning. Bravo!

Not a bad puzzle, if too easy for Friday (I solved it in Tuesday/Wednesday time). There were two many direct clues, but I enjoyed what little misdirection there was. Most of my difficulties had to do with trivia, but at least I found EL CLASICO a gimme. I'm not a football fan, but that is such a huge thing in Europe one simply can't be unfamiliar with it. In Polish a compact car (kompakt) is a hatchback by definition - a sedan would generally not be called kompakt over here (however, occasionally small city cars come in versions with boots stuck on awkwardly, like the Honda City once - a Honda Jazz with an additional, ugly boot section - and I suppose those are compact sedans...) Kajzerka ("the thing of the kajzer", more or less) was usually the only kind of roll available at stores before 1989 over here. These days it's still popular, and usually the cheapest roll offered by bakeries. It took me surprisingly long to type in SISYPHEAN - mostly because the English spelling looks alien to me. The guy is called Syzyf in Polish, and his hopeless task is described as SYZYFOWY. "Syzyfowe prace" (Sisyphean labours) is the title of a famous book by Stefan Żeromski, one of Poland's best writers of the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syzyfowe_prace - it captures the patriotism of Poles living under Russian rule in the late 19th century.

not sure if people realize just how good the 'fill' as they call it is in this puzzle - it's just one amazing conceit after another - it's literally on of the most beautiful puzzles I've ever seen - and I've been doing them for 30 years.  just look at the words and what they mean it's not cheap trivia or cheap words it's flat out Classic.
I liked this puzzle a lot! Plenty of interesting answers and clever clueing, and to me this is just about the right difficulty for a Friday puzzle.

there is on glaring and offensive clue - the latin for persona non grata does NOT MEAN the answer in the puzzle.  it never has it never will.  it's like saying someone with cancer or whatever disease is persona non grata - I imagine the constructor was talking about people who aim to hurt others and are then personal non grata.  call it what you will - don't blame the sick for health people's criminal actions

My first thought of "dogwalker" had me wondering if we were getting a Friday rebus. Not a huge fan of proper name answers but it's one way of learning new things, so...

The puzzle also brought to mind a new favorite quote: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy".
AFI? I like the double screening clue but that seemed to be a bit of a stretch. Am I crazy?
Good Wednesday puzzle

the Times better write up a tutorial on Latin translation PERSONA NON GRATA does not have anything to do with people who were sick - it ONLY means someone who meant to cause harm as a healthy individual and was cast out for their actions.  there is NO relationship between the two words not even casually - thanks ny times for shedding light on misconceptions that cause harm.
Pretty simple fill in the spaces while watching the sun rise in Ethiopia…. Hoped for something with a little more flesh in it for a Friday…

A Latin phrase meaning “unwelcome person.” As a legal term, it refers to the practice of a state prohibiting a diplomat from entering the country as a diplomat, or censuring a diplomat already resident in the country for conduct unbecoming of the status of a diplomat.

a Leper is not really that person they are sick with a disease - this is the meaning of the Latin - sadly most frat boys or ivy elites never bothered to learn the meaning of Latin - the most sacred of languages that allow us all to Speak Coherently across Centuries

I had no idea New York had so many lepers! 

High five to you all! (Oops, well, thumbs up, if you still got ‘em!)

I liked the Orinoco trivia, I didn't know it was such a beast...
However, to mention it even indirectly in the same breath as the Amazon is, quite frankly, an almost unforgivable insult.
The Amazon has a higher discharge than the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th largest rivers COMBINED.
Two of the Amazon's TRIBUTARIES would be in the top 6 largest rivers in the world by discharge if they were counted separately.
The 10 biggest rivers in Peru, a nation on the Pacific ocean, all eventually flow into the ATLANTIC ocean via the Amazon.
The Amazon is simply in a league of its own!
I liked that Class Acts and Relief Map were in the opposite corner from El Clasico and Sisyphean.

I know you’ll all say it was too easy, but I found yesterday a slog and was pleased to whip through this. Also, no matter the relative difficulty, Fridays have a different timbre to early-week puzzles. This felt nothing like a Wednesday despite being faster than many of those.
Plenty of a Friday puzzle for me. A good workout. Thank you.

A very trivia-heavy Friday that sadly got the better of me.

A lot of these answers have been 'banked' for future puzzles, and I'm quashing the frustration by treating this as a learning experience 🤣 😬. 

All in all, I felt this was an excellent, challenging puzzle. I always felt I was in with a fighting chance...

A person called Mother Teresa spent an entire lifetime trying to destigmatize leprosy and ensure that people with that disease were not treated as persona non grata. Even won a Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts. How poetic that we have a word like LEPER with such clever cluing on the eve of this year's Nobel Peace Prize.
Ali the gymnast added 10 minutes to today's solve time.

My refusal to think the answer for 16 A could possibly be what it ended up being (shame, shame, editors) along with NERF dArt, slowed me down a little in the NE, but I got that sorted out.

So, it was all going to come down to one square.  LEmAY seemed like the most likely name considering that King Arthur trivia is not my FORTe.

Now, I may not know Latin, but even *I* know the relationship between "mort" and death, so that didn't seem to fit the clue.

FORTe!  Strength!  Yes, I think I've got it!

What a RELIEF!
AFORTIORI did me in.

Do you feel good about yourself? 
Aforti-whatever, pak, spirograph ,plus about 20 proper nouns... I would have gone to the pub last night if I wanted a mega dose of trivia. Such snob-bish construction. Thanks for nothing.
Loved, loved, loved it. Fantastic fill. Sometimes a puzzle goes so far up my alley that it really ought to have a back-up alarm.

Poor Erik Satie! Today, known mainly for his three Gymnopédies (Satie often wrote in sets of three, almost identical, pieces) and a Gnossienne or two--where would freelance wedding harpists be without them?--his work was much more broad-ranging than that. From his early mystical works: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8CX1NSswGZQ&list=RD8CX1NSswGZQ&start_radio=1 (talk about EGO: "I dedicate this work to myself"; in reality, Satie was anything but egoistic, merely sarcastic.") To his later, satirical works, some of which even @Captain Quahog would approve: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzuWmVaUoFw&list=RDrzuWmVaUoFw&start_radio=1 (Bonus points if you can read the French in the scores.) (both recordings by Jean-Yves Thibaudet.) *** Get that wax out of you ears, kids! Here's a Song to the Siren, by Jeff Buckley, performed live on . . . the Monkees!: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vaa22ULitds&list=RDvaa22ULitds&start_radio=1 And here's a brilliant cover by Elizabeth Fraser, of Dead Can Dance: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HFWKJ2FUiAQ&list=RDHFWKJ2FUiAQ&start_radio=1

Obscure, to say the least. Fridays usually sit empty for awhile and then fill, because of the multi-worded answers and requirement for deep thinking. It's my favorite puzzle day of the week. This puzzle? This was an absurd overuse of random names to fill a grid, requiring knowledge of abstruse trivia - and certainly not contemplation. 

I'll go back to the archives for my Friday fix.

It’s been more than four years since we’ve seen Nam in the Times, and he’s continued where he left off without losing a step.  

Nam’s cleverness in clue and beauty in answer in the past -- such as [Needle exchange?] for FRIENDLY BANTER (2022) -- continually charmed me.  And here it is again today.  I especially liked the second word in [Device geared to draw rotationally symmetrical shapes] for SPIROGRAPH (a NYT debut, BTW).

Another NYT debut – today’s grid design – provided for an amazingly high 20 longs (answers of eight letters or more), and man, did Nam pack in the quality.  CLASS ACTS, WHIPPETS, WELL TO DO, SISYPHEAN, SIREN SONG, ON THE ROPES,  SPIROGRAPH, and more. 

Beauty like that transforms the box into a gem.

The NW gave me the kind of fight my brain loves, and there were several splat-fills to provide “whee!”.  I also liked DOG crossing DANE (as in Great).

But, to me, the beauty ruled today, and it greatly enriched my day, Nam.  Welcome back, and thank you!

The clue for 35 down was cheeky and hilarious! A super-long delightfully easy to guess quote (it even name drops "Vader") in the middle of a Friday puzzle! It was such an over-the-top gimme that I laughed out loud when I came to it. Lovely placement!

In a well crafted puzzle like this one, rather than seeming like “random trivia”,  unknown-to-me clues and answers like 56A (the soccer game) come across as interesting things to discover, and also another bit of evidence that these puzzle-makers have mastered the craft of making things dicey but do-able. I believe that one, and Wong Kar-Wai, were the only two I found completely new, but lots of others were only remotely familiar and allowed for a similar, pleasingly-gradual remembrance. And the ‘oh, yeah’ is not always in the answers - sometimes the clues are what teach us, or remind us, of noteworthy facts. For example, it had completely slipped my mind that the 21st word of that line by Princess Leia was “brought”. 

Nice puzzle.

This one defeated me.  It’s funny because I am definitely in the “Make the themeless puzzles hard again” camp, and then when I am presented with things I don’t know crossing with spellings I am not sure of I get so annoyed.  I guess I can’t have it both ways!  Glad I no longer agonize over flyspecking in an attempt to keep a meaningless streak alive - one like this would have affected my mood for most of the day a couple of years ago.  Well done to those of you for whom this wasn’t as much of a challenge, and best wishes for a great long weekend!

Theme clues and answers: "90" PARENTHESES "3" POUNDSIGN "1" EXCLAMATIONMARK "7" AMPERSAND And then the reveal: "What is being held in 17-, 32-, 38- and 45-across" THESHIFTKEY Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=9/27/2007&h=38a ....

On LEPER.  I have always used this term, not that I've had occasion to use it in this way very often, in a sardonically figurative way to express the idea that I feel like a leper because of the way I'm being treated.  It's a species of hyperbole.  I'm also happy to report that no one has ever accused me of being insensitive to the plight of people suffering from leprosy.
Am I the only one unable to access the easy mode puzzle? I click on the links but they take me to the main puzzle page. What am I overlooking?

We've all had this stress dream, yes?  You're being given an exam in a class that you never attended and for which you've done no reading at all.  That's how I felt trying to do this puzzle.

Boy, was I not having fun!  All these tiny pieces of unrelated and unfamiliar info I was expected to know, but didn't.  If I managed to finish this -- and I'd definitely need to cheat, at least a bit -- would I feel smart?  I suspect I'd just feel tired and put upon.

So I stopped.  I do that a lot these days.  No sense in suffering needlessly, that's what I say.  And please note that today I didn't put "suffering" in quotes -- a dead giveaway to how I'm really feeling about a puzzle deep inside.  In case you couldn't figure it out, that is:)

Puzzle of the year candidate? It’s a strong contender!

Hats off to you, Nam Jin Yoon, for bestowing a sweet solve like this on an otherwise unassuming Friday morning.

Lots of fun wordplay here, spanning lots of categories while doing a respectable job avoiding crossing proper nouns. Even though I couldn't remember if it was spelled with an I or a Y, I particularly enjoyed finally recalling the name of a SPIROGRAPH. Nice Friday.

Six years ago today - and on a Friday - my daughter was born. We were in the throes of the pandemic, yet her arrival inspired a sense of hope, beauty, and joy in contrast to the darkness and uncertainty of that time. We were enamored, and overjoyed to welcome her into our lives even with the difficulty inherent to starting a family at that time. (Grateful too for our many blessings and privileges even with those challenges.) In the relatively quiet isolation of that time, my crossword solving habit kicked off. 6 years old today she inspires me still! Watching her grow continues to be a source of both challenge and pride.  And so too, for my solving habit! I went from using auto check on early-week puzzles to a nearly 400 day streak. Thank you to the constructors who provide this solace and challenge during the uncertainties we  all may be facing.
Hope you like this as much as I do: https://youtu.be/JSwQ-b3zE1M?is=5CZKKy87qsR9xt1x. In case the link doesn’t work, go to YouTube and search “Orinoco Flow”.
A fun workout.  Well done and thanks.

Man that was tricky, even by late-week standards. I got there eventually, but the SE corner came down to multiple guesses. I think it I had one crossword wish granted, it'd be for no more sports clues - once you get beyond a handful of famous names, it's almost uniformly trivia I never know from outside the puzzle and just have to hope that the crossing clues are enough to go on.

I read the comment:
 "Ideally, crosswords incorporate a diverse range of trivia and cultural references into the grid."
and was astonished! "Ideally"? Is this true?

If I'd known this when I first considered subscribing to NYT crosswords, I never would have started. I think trivia (brand names no longer in use) and cultural references can sometimes be the most tiresome and tedious aspect of the crossword. And it's not just because it's mostly American - I feel the same about British trivia. 

I enjoyed today's offering though. Not too tricky.

My late father (who was born in 1928) once told me he didn’t know what all the fuss about Native American iconography in sports was. I told him that it wasn’t up to us but up to Native Americans to decide what is offensive to them. And that we’d be horrified if a team had a mascot in blackface or yellowface. He told me he understood. So it’s up to the people with Hansen’s disease to decide whether the term leper is derogatory. And they have. So perhaps the Times could find alternatives? https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2021/jul/12/health-campaigners-call-for-an-end-to-the-use-of-the-word-leper Ps. I served in the Peace Corps in West Africa and saw people with serious cases of Hansen disease. They were ostracized enough without more help from us. PPS. My wife and I visited Kalaupapa NHS on Molokai where Father Damien ministered to people with Hansen disease who were exiled there. In the early 1980s a state legislator in Hawaii seriously proposed sending people with HIV there.

I just don’t see the entry “Persona non grata => LEPER” in today’s puzzle as taking any kind of value stance.

It’s certainly not saying that people with leprosy *should* be ostracized, or viewed as morally culpable of their disease, or anything along those lines.

Perhaps your argument is more that, by simply publishing that entry, the NYT is complicit (regardless of intent) in perpetuating a meaning/association that should be stricken from the popular lexicon.

As I see it, the term’s presence in major English translations of the Christian Bible alone guarantees it will outlive both of us in the popular lexicon; and apart from Biblical references, “leper” is used almost exclusively for hyperbole (“treated me like a leper”) in contemporary contexts (in American English, the primary/default language of NYT crossword puzzles).

I can understand why your personal experiences would have left you with very different (and much more vivid) associations with/feelings about “leper” than the term invokes for the average NYT crossword solver, but you can’t please everybody.
